extracted.intended_audience: people who write captions for cartoon caption contests (esp. New Yorker contestants), gag writers and aspiring humor caption writers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing short, effective gag captions for cartoon caption contests (with emphasis on The New Yorker contest): how to choose voice, craft wording, balance predictability, and iterate submissions to improve chances of winning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity / word limit
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep captions short — historically contests have imposed word limits (e.g., “must not exceed sixteen words in all — the shorter the better”).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short captions are preferred; economical wording often reads punchier. The historical rule ‘the shorter the better’ is explicitly cited as good advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who's Talking (speaker identification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be clear about the speaker or 'who's talking' in the caption — determine the voice or perspective that best fits the drawing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of the book's chapter headings is “Who’s Talking,” implying that choosing an apt speaker/persona for the line helps create humor and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: What's Happening (action/scene alignment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand and reference ‘what’s happening’ in the cartoon — align your caption to the action or situation depicted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A chapter titled “What’s Happening” emphasizes anchoring the gag in the observable scene so the caption connects logically (or amusingly subverts) the visual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tell a Story
rubrics_metrics.description: Good captions often tell a tiny story rather than a one-word gag — they imply context, cause, or consequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A one- or two-line micro-narrative can give the caption weight and make the payoff stronger; the book includes a chapter called “Tell a Story.”

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose Your Words Carefully
rubrics_metrics.description: Precise word choice and phrasing matter — small differences in wording can determine whether a line wins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chapter “Choose Your Words Carefully.” Example shown where near-duplicate lines (‘I give no quarter.’ / ‘I give you no quarter.’ / ‘I will give you no quarter.’) only one specific phrasing was chosen; subtle differences can be decisive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance Predictability and Surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid being too predictable and avoid being so unpredictable that the joke doesn't land — find the sweet spot between obvious and obscure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two chapter titles, “Don’t Be Too Predictable” and “Don’t Be Too Unpredictable,” explicitly advise finding the right balance so the gag is fresh but accessible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take the Drawing to Unexpected Places (creative leap)
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful captions often take the drawing in an unexpected direction, offering a surprising interpretation or twist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Farley Katz's quote: he loves seeing caption writers 'take my drawings to entirely new and unexpected places.' This creative leap is valued by cartoonists and contest editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterate and Test Entries (work up multiple variations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare several alternate captions for the same cartoon and get feedback from friends/family to choose the best.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part Three suggests working up a few entries and having others judge; try multiple formulations and solicit outside opinion to avoid ego bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submit Often / Persistence
rubrics_metrics.description: Persistence and volume of submissions increase chances of success — prolific entrants accumulate more wins/finalist placements over time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lawrence Wood sent in over 800 gags and accumulated many wins and finalist spots; being prolific and persistent is implied as a path to eventual success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leave Your Ego Behind / Handle Rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept that good lines may lose and that editors choose based on taste; avoid obsessing over a perceived better line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part Three, “Winning Isn’t Everything,” advises leaving ego behind; many entries similar to yours may be submitted and editors will pick the line they prefer for subtle reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be Aware of Common or Near-Duplicate Lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Many contestants submit very similar jokes; being aware of common tropes helps you avoid obvious duplicates that diminish chances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review cites an example where a cartoon drew more than 200 similar lines; uniqueness and a distinctive phrasing can help your entry stand out among many near-duplicates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect Cartoonists' Preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all cartoonists want their drawings used in caption contests; be aware some artists dislike captions written by outsiders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sam Gross's quote: 'You will never see one of my cartoons in the contest... I don’t want some dentist in Toledo captioning my work.' This indicates sensitivity around artistic intent and the relationship between cartoonist and caption-writer.
